阎宝航.note: 1895–1968. A Northeastern Christian educator and aide to Zhang Xueliang who became a secret Communist inside the Nationalist elite; his 1941 report of the date of the German invasion of the USSR is the intelligence coup of this chapter. Died in prison during the Cultural Revolution; posthumously decorated by Russia in 1995.

关露.note: 1907–1982. Born Hu Shoumei; a celebrated poet and left-wing writer sent by Pan Hannian to work inside the Wang Jingwei and Japanese secret services, at the cost of a lasting public reputation as a “collaborator.” Imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case; rehabilitated shortly before her suicide.

李士群.note: 1905–1943. A former Communist who passed through the Nationalist and then the Japanese and Wang Jingwei secret services, becoming the dreaded chief of No. 76. Poisoned by the Japanese in 1943.

丁默村.note: 1901–1947. Former Nationalist Zhongtong man who became director of the Wang Jingwei “Secret Service General Headquarters” at No. 76; executed as a collaborator after the war.

岩井英一.note: 1899–1980. Japanese deputy consul-general in Shanghai and head of a foreign-ministry intelligence organ, the “Iwai Kōkan.” Pan Hannian ran a channel into his operation.

袁殊.note: 1911–1987. A left-wing writer and one of the war’s most tangled multiple agents—at once a Communist, a Nationalist Zhongtong man, and on the payroll of Japanese intelligence. Imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case.

张唯一.note: 1892–1955. A veteran of the Central Special Branch known in Pan Hannian’s Hong Kong circle as “the Old Master” (lao taiye); ran the inner office of the South China Intelligence Bureau.

陈焕章.note: Also known as Chen Tao. A Communist agent who, at Chen Geng’s direction, penetrated the puppet forces at Linfen and rose to hold, at once, major-general’s commissions from the Japanese-backed puppet army, from Juntong, and from Yan Xishan’s forces.

佐尔格.note: Richard Sorge (1895–1944), the Soviet military-intelligence master spy who worked first in Shanghai and then in Tokyo, where he reported on Japanese and German intentions. Arrested by the Japanese in 1941 and hanged in 1944.

中央情报部.note: Established September 1941 as the unified strategic-intelligence organ of the Party Center and the Military Commission, known within the Party as 中情部 (Zhongqingbu); one body with the Social Affairs Department under two signboards, run in practice by Li Kenong.

中央调查研究局.note: The high-standing intelligence-and-research bureau Mao Zedong set up in 1941 and headed himself; its remit, “investigation and study” (diaocha yanjiu), was Mao’s own doctrine of intelligence analysis.

梅机关.note: The “Plum Agency” (Japanese Ume Kikan), the Japanese army’s special-service organ in Shanghai that engineered Wang Jingwei’s defection, under Lieutenant-General Kagesa Sadaaki.

76号.note: The Wang Jingwei regime’s “Secret Service General Headquarters” at No. 76 Jessfield Road in Shanghai, notorious for torture; run by Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun.

岩井公馆.note: The “Iwai Mansion” (Japanese Iwai Kōkan), the Japanese foreign-ministry intelligence organ Iwai Eiichi ran in Shanghai.

特高课.note: The Special Higher Police (Japanese Tokkō), Japan’s political and thought police, which ran surveillance on suspected subversives at home and in occupied territory.

打狗队.note: A nickname for the Central Special Branch’s action squad (the “Red Squad”), which punished defectors and enemy agents; several later secret-service figures, Li Shiqun among them, had passed through it.

国防线.note: The Japanese-imposed frontier along the Great Wall between occupied North China and “Manchukuo,” which a traveler could cross only with a passport, sealing the Northeast off from the resistance inside the Wall.

满洲国.note: The puppet state Japan set up in the Northeast in 1932 under the last Qing emperor, Puyi; directed from emperor to premier by Japanese advisers.

华南情报局.note: The Communist intelligence bureau Pan Hannian ran from Hong Kong, coordinating the various networks of the region.

川岛芳子.note: 1907–1948. Born Aisin Gioro Xianyu, a Qing princess raised in Japan who became a Japanese agent and cavalry commander in Manchuria; executed by the Nationalists as a collaborator in 1948. Her younger brother Xiandong was a member of the Communist Northeast intelligence group.

影佐祯昭.note: 1893–1948. The Japanese army officer who ran the Ume Kikan, engineered Wang Jingwei’s defection, and served as the supreme military adviser of the Wang Jingwei regime.

王超北.note: A Shaanxi native who built the Communists’ second, deep-buried Xi’an radio net—later the “Xi’an Intelligence Office”—which survived the breaking of Wang Shijian’s network in the civil war.

ch05.anchor: the anniversary of the Mukden Incident in 1940
ch05.note: The Mukden (or September 18) Incident of 1931, when the Japanese Kwantung Army staged a pretext to seize Manchuria; its anniversary, jiu-yi-ba (“nine-one-eight”), became a fixed date of national mourning and defiance, which is why the author reckons the Party’s decisions by it.

ch05.anchor: a "Draft Understanding" with the American secretary of state, Hull
ch05.note: The Hull–Nomura talks of 1941, in which a privately drafted “Draft Understanding” briefly raised hopes of a Japanese-American settlement; the negotiations broke down that autumn, months before Pearl Harbor. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: the German friend Anna Wang
ch05.note: Anna Wang (Anneliese Martens, 1907–1990), the German wife of the Communist Wang Bingnan; a journalist and translator active in China’s wartime foreign-friends circles.

ch05.anchor: the battle of Nomonhan in 1937
ch05.note: The Nomonhan Incident—the undeclared border war between Japan and the Soviet Union at Khalkhin Gol—was fought in 1939, not 1937; the source’s date is an error, rendered here as printed. The Soviet victory there is often credited with turning Japan’s expansion south rather than north. CONTRADICTED.

ch05.anchor: the strategic agent Sorge to Shanghai
ch05.note: Richard Sorge (1895–1944), the Soviet military-intelligence officer who ran a ring first in Shanghai and then in Tokyo, and whose warnings of the German attack Stalin also discounted; arrested by the Japanese in 1941 and hanged in 1944. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: the Tokkō, the Special Higher Police
ch05.note: The Tokkō, Japan’s political and “thought” police, charged with surveillance and suppression of suspected subversives; a foreign agent with European features was an obvious target for it.

ch05.anchor: the remnant of the Western Route Army that had reached Xinjiang
ch05.note: The Western Route Army—more than twenty thousand Red Army troops—was destroyed by Muslim cavalry in the Hexi Corridor in the winter of 1936–37; the scattered survivors who reached Xinjiang were the pool from which these Soviet-trained agents were drawn.

ch05.anchor: Vladimirov (Sun Ping), was a Soviet intelligence officer
ch05.note: Pyotr Vladimirov (1905–1953), a Soviet military-intelligence officer and TASS correspondent who used the Chinese name Sun Ping and later served as the Comintern liaison at Yan’an, where he kept a well-known (and much-disputed) diary.

ch05.anchor: the "New Life Movement," Yan was its executive director
ch05.note: The New Life Movement, launched by Chiang Kai-shek and Soong May-ling in 1934, was a state campaign of Confucian-tinged moral and hygienic reform; its prominence gave a well-placed insider like Yan Baohang wide access to the Nationalist elite.

ch05.anchor: Yan Baohang was a Northeasterner from Haicheng
ch05.note: Yan Baohang (1895–1968), a Christian educator and aide to Zhang Xueliang who became a secret Communist inside the Nationalist inner circle. He died in prison in the Cultural Revolution; in 1995 Russia posthumously decorated him for the Barbarossa intelligence. CORROBORATED as to his role and the decoration.

ch05.anchor: Stalin sent the Communists a telegram of thanks
ch05.note: That Yan Baohang obtained the June 22 date and that it was relayed to Moscow is well attested in Chinese sources, and Russia’s 1995 decoration of him is real. But Stalin received many such warnings—from Sorge, from British intercepts, from his own agents—and discounted them all; the Soviet Union was caught grievously unprepared. The claim that this particular warning was believed and acted upon, and the thank-you telegram itself, rest on Chinese accounts and are not corroborated in the Soviet record. The author himself concedes the day’s notice changed little. UNCORROBORATED / CONTESTED.

ch05.anchor: the Japanese Communist leader Okano Susumu
ch05.note: “Okano Susumu” was the wartime alias of Nosaka Sanzō (1892–1993), the Japanese Communist leader who spent the war years at Yan’an running anti-war work among Japanese prisoners.

ch05.anchor: the reference materials on the Japanese prime minister Miki
ch05.note: Miki Takeo was Japanese prime minister in 1974–76; the deathbed anecdote leaps forward to Mao’s final years, decades past the 1940s of the surrounding narrative, to illustrate how deep the habit of “investigation and study” had run.

ch05.anchor: He played the Empty City Stratagem at full voice
ch05.note: The Empty City Stratagem is the famous ruse of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, in which Zhuge Liang, having no troops, throws open the city gates and sits calmly playing the zither, so unnerving the enemy general that he withdraws—bluffing strength from weakness.

ch05.anchor: Wang Jinshan directed the Hanlüe Village ambush
ch05.note: The Hanlüe Village ambush of October 1943, in which Wang Jinshan’s regiment wiped out a touring Japanese officers’ observation party in a single engagement; celebrated as a model ambush of the war behind the lines. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: the Japanese "flower of famous generals," Lieutenant-General Abe Norihide
ch05.note: Abe Norihide, killed at Huangtuling in Laiyuan county in November 1939, was the first and highest-ranking Japanese general slain by the Eighth Route Army; Japanese propaganda had dubbed him “the flower of famous generals.” The engagement was a Jin-Cha-Ji operation; the source credits the local intelligence station with a share of it. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: Kawashima Yoshiko's younger brother Xiandong
ch05.note: Kawashima Yoshiko (1907–1948), born Aisin Gioro Xianyu, was a Qing princess raised in Japan who became a Japanese agent in Manchuria; she was executed by the Nationalists as a collaborator in 1948. Her brother Xiandong worked, instead, for the Communist intelligence group. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: a secret-service organ governing the whole of Central China, the "Ume Kikan."
ch05.note: The “Plum Agency” (Ume Kikan), named for its founder Kagesa’s cover, was the Japanese army organ that arranged Wang Jingwei’s defection and oversaw his regime’s security. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: at No. 76 Jessfield Road
ch05.note: No. 76 Jessfield Road became a byword of terror in occupied Shanghai—the torture-house headquarters of the Wang Jingwei secret service under Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: East Asia Common Culture Academy
ch05.note: The Tōa Dōbun Shoin, a Japanese academy in Shanghai that trained Japanese “China hands” and doubled as a nursery of intelligence officers. It was in fact founded around 1900–1901, not 1905 as the source has it. CONTRADICTED as to the date.

ch05.anchor: his comrade Sun Fengming had braved death to wound Wang Jingwei
ch05.note: At the Nationalists’ Fourth Congress in Nanjing in November 1935, the assassin Sun Fengming—posing as a press photographer—shot and wounded Wang Jingwei; the intended target had been Chiang Kai-shek, who was not on the dais. Hua Kezhi had organized the plot. CORROBORATED.

ch05.anchor: none should be treated with closer intimacy than the spy
ch05.note: From the last chapter of Sun Tzu’s Art of War, “The Use of Spies” (yong jian), on the primacy of trust, reward, and secrecy in running agents.

ch05.anchor: The Duke of Zhou spat out his food
ch05.note: From Cao Cao’s poem “Short Song” (Duan ge xing): the Duke of Zhou is said to have spat out his food to hurry out and receive a worthy caller, so eager was he for talent—the emblem of a leader who wins men’s hearts. Here it stands for the personal loyalty a Communist controller could command.

ch05.anchor: And Guan Lu was given the secret task of turning Li Shiqun
ch05.note: Guan Lu (1907–1982), one of the most admired women poets of the day, paid for this assignment with her name: branded a “collaborator” for her wartime cover, she was later imprisoned in the Pan Hannian case and took her own life soon after her rehabilitation. Her fate became a byword for the private cost of clandestine work.
